match.reason: Neither bank point teaches why readers prefer certain texts through features like genre, pace, characters and voice; both cover how historical context and readers' values shape meaning and interpretation, which is a different idea.

draft.title: Why readers prefer certain texts
card: Genre
the type of text, such as mystery, fantasy or romance. Readers often prefer genres whose patterns they enjoy.
Pace
how fast events unfold. Some readers like quick action, while others like slow, detailed build-up.
Characters
readers often prefer texts with characters they care about, because they want to know what happens to them.
Voice
the distinctive way a narrator or writer sounds, such as funny, blunt or poetic. A strong voice can draw some readers in and put others off.
draft.remember: Genre, pace, characters and voice help explain why a text suits some readers and not others.

a.q: Priya loves stories where the narrator speaks in a sharp, funny way that feels like a friend talking. Which feature appeals to her?
a.why: The sharp, funny way the narrator sounds is the voice. Pace is about how fast events move, and nothing in the example says the story is fast.
a.clue: Think about how the narrator sounds.

b.q: Tom puts down a long fantasy novel because very little happens in the first hundred pages. Which feature best explains why the book does not suit him?
opts: Its pace is slower than he likes
Its genre is fantasy, which no reader enjoys
Its voice is the same as every other novel
b.why: Tom is bothered that little happens for a long time, which is about pace. Fantasy is a genre that many readers enjoy, so genre alone does not explain his reaction. Nothing is said about the characters or voice.
b.clue: Focus on what Tom says about events.

b.best: Its pace is slower than he likes

problems.detail: Every wrong option uses an absolute claim ('always unlikeable', 'which no reader enjoys', 'the same as every other novel'), while the right option is the only reasonable, qualified statement. A student can pick it by spotting the absolutes, without knowing what pace means.
The option 'Its characters are always unlikeable' uses 'always', but the card says readers 'often' prefer certain characters and uses hedged language throughout.
The clue says 'Focus on what Tom says about events', but Tom says nothing in the question. The stem only describes why he puts the book down.

check.summary: The card and question a are sound. In question b, all three wrong options are absolute overstatements (always, no reader, every other), so the right answer stands out without knowing the idea. The clue also wrongly says Tom 'says' something.
